Spainâs marbled duck recovery highlights how sustained wetland restoration, captive breeding and cooperation among conservation groups can help rebuild threatened bird populations.How Spainâs marbled duck breeding numbers changed between 2009 and 2025The marbled duck (Marmaronetta angustirostris), also known as the marbled teal, is a wetland bird found across parts of the Mediterranean region, North Africa and Asia. In Spain, its breeding population declined sharply, reaching just 20 pairs in 2009. Conservation efforts have since focused on protecting the wetlands the species needs to breed and feed. Spain recorded 130 females with broods and 806 chicks in 2024. Co-financed by the EU LIFE programme and Spainâs Directorate-General for Water, the project combined restoration work with species monitoring, captive breeding and agreements with local stakeholders. Work at these sites included improvements to water management and measures to provide suitable habitat for breeding birds.Elsewhere, restoration work in the Brazo del Este Natural Area in Seville covered 24 hectares and, together with two rehabilitated meanders of a former branch of the Guadalquivir River, created 50 hectares in total. These voluntary arrangements support cooperation in the management and protection of natural habitats.Researchers tracked 164 birds fitted with GPS/GSM transmitters to investigate movement patterns, survival and habitat use. The project identified more than 60 wetlands used by the species and developed measures to address threats including accidental hunting, poaching and disease outbreaks associated with botulism and cyanobacteria. Habitat loss and degradation, disturbance, climate change and hunting in parts of its range remain concerns.
